title: How much water is on Earth?
narration: What if all Earth’s ocean water vanished instantly? You’ve probably never imagined how much water the planet actually holds. The hydrosphere contains 1.386 billion cubic kilometres of water. That includes every river, lake, glacier, and air moisture. Saltwater makes up 97.5 percent of that total. Fresh water is just 2.5 percent. Oceans cover about 71 percent of Earth’s surface. That area is roughly 361 million square kilometres. It is larger than all land combined. When you look at a map, most blue is ocean. The numbers show 1.386 billion cubic kilometres of water. Ninety-seven and a half percent is salty. The immediate loss of water is next.

title: 97.5% of water just gone
narration: Picture the ocean’s blue blanket vanishing in an instant. What happens to the water budget? Suddenly, 97.5 percent of the planet’s water disappears. The saltwater ocean is gone. Only the fresh fraction remains. Your planet is left with just 2.5 percent of its original water. Most of that tiny slice is locked as ice or trapped deep in groundwater. Only about 0.3 percent of fresh water lives in lakes and rivers you can easily reach. The total hydrosphere mass is about 1.4 times ten to the eighteenth tonnes. Think of an Olympic pool holding 2,500 tonnes. The next step shows exactly how this sudden drop impacts your daily water access.

title: Is the air still wet?
narration: The oceans are gone, so what floats above you now? At any moment, about 2 times ten to the thirteenth tonnes of water sit as vapor in the atmosphere. That is a huge cloud of moisture, even without seas. You might think the air empties out. But water does not disappear. It only moves. The hydrosphere is a closed system. Vapor stays aloft because water molecules remain there. This means the sky still holds a thin blanket of water. You can still feel humidity on your skin. Clouds still form because the vapor is not destroyed. Water is neither created nor destroyed. It only migrates. The vapor stays.
